question:
The predictive ability of a polygenic score, measured by variance explained, is necessarily lower than the SNP heritability for the phenotype. Answer with one of the following:
True
False

2.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: True. The SNP heritability represents the total proportion of phenotypic variance that can be tagged by all measured SNPs in aggregate, but a polygenic score is a finite weighted sum of a subset of those SNPs whose effect sizes are estimated with noise from finite samples. This estimation error, imperfect tagging due to LD, and the need to apply shrinkage or clumping inevitably means the out-of-sample R² achieved by any practical PGS will fall short of the SNP-heritability upper bound.

3.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is defined as the fraction of phenotypic variance that is collectively explained by all SNPs (i.e., the additive genetic variance tagged by the SNP set). A polygenic score is a linear combination of a finite number of estimated SNP effect sizes; because those estimates are obtained from finite samples they contain noise, the set of SNPs retained is usually incomplete or pruned, and linkage disequilibrium prevents perfect tagging of causal variants. Consequently the out-of-sample \(R^2\) achieved by any PGS is bounded above by \(h^2_{SNP}\) and, except in degenerate limiting cases that are never realized in practice, is strictly smaller. The inequality is therefore necessary.

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is defined as the proportion of phenotypic variance captured by the additive genetic contribution of all measured (or imputed) SNPs; it is exactly the \(R^2\) that would be obtained by the optimal linear predictor that uses every SNP with its true effect size. A polygenic score is constructed from estimated, noisy effect sizes obtained from a finite GWAS and is therefore a noisy, imperfect proxy for that optimal predictor. Consequently its out-of-sample \(R^2\) is strictly smaller than \(h^2_{SNP}\) except in the unattainable limit of infinite sample size and perfect knowledge of all effect sizes. The inequality is therefore necessary.

(The statement refers only to variance explained; it does not address other metrics such as AUC or calibration that can behave differently.)

2.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: True. These biases are intrinsic to any realizable GWAS-based predictor, so the out-of-sample R² is necessarily strictly below h²_SNP.

public_text.1:
True

The group consensus is already exhaustive and mutually reinforcing: \(h^2_{SNP}\) is the population \(R^2\) of the unobserved oracle linear predictor using every SNP at its exact causal effect. Every realizable PGS is strictly inferior because of finite-sample estimation error, imperfect LD tagging, pruning/regularization losses, winner’s-curse bias, shrinkage, residual stratification, portability mismatches (LD/AF/environment), and any unmodeled nonlinear/GxE terms still present in broader SNP-heritability definitions. These gaps are intrinsic; they vanish only in the unattainable infinite-\(N\), perfect-LD, population-matched limit. No counter-example or alternative metric has been supplied that would allow equality under the variance-explained definition, so the strict inequality remains necessarily true.
public_text.2: True. Adding to the measurement-error and reference-panel points already latent in our discussion, even an idealized linear PGS faces an irreducible ceiling from imperfect phenotype ascertainment (e.g., noisy clinical diagnoses, batch effects in biomarkers, or right-censored survival traits). Because SNP-heritability estimators recover the latent liability or liability-scale variance that includes this measurement component, while any deployed score is trained and evaluated on the noisier observed phenotype, the attainable out-of-sample R² is strictly bounded below h²_SNP under every realistic data-generating process. This gap persists after all finite-sample, LD, and stratification corrections have been idealized away, reinforcing the necessity of the inequality.
